The model decomposes each shift into components representing offensive and defensive contributions (β_j, δ_j), zone-start effects (ζ_off, ζ_def), and intercept (β_0). This structure enables estimation of net player impact on scoring events while adjusting for confounding variables such as teammates, opponents, and starting zone. The use of proxy outcomes—shots, Fenwick, Corsi—is justified by their strong correlation with goals and ability to provide more frequent measurements than raw goal data. These proxies are rescaled using league-average conversion rates to yield expected goals per 60 minutes, ensuring comparability across contexts. Ridge regression introduces a penalty term λβ^Tβ to stabilize coefficient estimates, particularly important when dealing with high-dimensional feature spaces where traditional OLS suffers from instability due to collinearity. The choice of λ ≈ 0.5 balances model complexity and generalization based on empirical validation curves. The failure mode arises when data lacks sufficient variation or when assumptions about linearity and stationarity are violated, leading to unreliable estimates.
